title: Amen (CCC 1061–1065)
hook: the Creed ends as scripture does: Amen, Christ himself is the Amen

segments.voice: Yesterday, a new heaven and earth: creation renewed, not thrown away. Your line was all things new. Today, the last word of the Creed.

"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you all. Amen." That's the last verse of the Bible in the Douay-Rheims, and its last word is the one the Creed ends on too. The Creed opens with I believe and travels a long way: God, Christ, the Spirit, the Church, forgiveness, the resurrection, life everlasting. Then a whole church closes it with that small word. For days now, this path has walked through the first part of the Catechism, what Catholics believe. The Catechism closes that part the way the Creed does.
screen: `THE BIBLE'S LAST WORD.` → `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` → `ONE SMALL WORD.`

segments.voice: The Great Amen at Mass came up on day one hundred fifteen; today, the word itself. First, what it is. In Hebrew, the Catechism explains, amen shares its root with the word for believing. It carries the sense of something solid, trustworthy, faithful, something you can lean your weight on. So amen isn't just I agree. It's this holds. Second, God first. In the prophet Isaiah, God himself is called the God of truth, which in Hebrew is the God of amen. People can say amen to God's promises because God is faithful first. Third, a bookend. The Creed's last word, the Catechism says, repeats and confirms its first: I believe. It quotes Saint Augustine, who told new Christians to let the Creed be a kind of mirror, something to look into every day to see whether they still believe what they say. Fourth, the Amen has a name. In the Apocalypse, Christ introduces himself to a church like this, in the Douay-Rheims: "These things saith the Amen, the faithful and true witness." Not someone who says amen. The Amen. Saint Paul writes that all God's promises find their yes in Christ. In Catholic belief, Christ is God's final, faithful yes to the world, and when people say amen, they join their small yes to his. So the word at the end of the Creed isn't a full stop. It's a signature: everything above this line, I'm leaning my weight on it.
screen: `SOLID, TRUSTWORTHY, FAITHFUL.` · `THE GOD OF AMEN.` · `I BELIEVE … AMEN.` · `THESE THINGS SAITH THE AMEN.`

segments.voice: Breathe in, and on the way out say the word quietly, or in your head, stretched long: amen. Say it again, and this time let it mean what the Catechism says it means: this holds. If you pray, say it to God about something you trust him with; if you don't, let it be a yes to something true in your life, a person, a promise, a place that has held you up.
Amen. A Hebrew word for what is solid and faithful, the last word of the Creed, and, in the Apocalypse, a name for Christ himself. Today's word.
Your line: so be it. A small word that can hold a whole life's weight. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics say amen at the end of the Creed, after prayers at Mass, and when receiving Communion, when the minister says "the Body of Christ" and each person answers amen.

chat.says: Why does everyone say amen at the end? Isn't it just how prayers stop?
options: It means this holds: it shares a root with believing, so it's a yes, not a full stop.
It's a Latin word meaning the end, so it simply tells everyone the prayer is over.

chat.meaning: The Catechism says amen shares its Hebrew root with believing: something solid you can lean on. In the Apocalypse, Christ himself is called the Amen.
